findings.source_passage: Even in Broadway and Chestnut streets, Mediterranean mariners will sometimes jostle the affrighted ladies. Regent Street is not unknown to Lascars and Malays; and at Bombay, in the Apollo Green, live Yankees have often scared the natives.
findings.source_locator: Paragraph 2, before 'But New Bedford beats all Water Street and Wapping'
findings.why_it_matters: This comic geographical catalogue — Broadway, Chestnut, Regent Street, Bombay — establishes the chapter's satirical, globe-trotting swagger before the punchline 'But New Bedford beats all.' Its removal kills the rhetorical buildup and the ironic cosmopolitanism that is the chapter's distinctive voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the Broadway/Chestnut/Regent Street/Bombay sequence as a compressed single sentence before the 'beats all Water Street and Wapping' line to preserve the rhetorical arc.

findings.source_passage: No town-bred dandy will compare with a country-bred one—I mean a downright bumpkin dandy—a fellow that, in the dog-days, will mow his two acres in buckskin gloves for fear of tanning his hands.
findings.source_locator: Paragraph 4, opening of the 'country dandy' digression
findings.why_it_matters: The 'bumpkin dandy' definition is the chapter's most distinctly satirical voice-passage; the buckskin-gloves detail is classic Melvillean comic specificity. The draft jumps to 'Ah, poor Hay-Seed!' without the setup, flattening the narrator's ironic persona and losing the joke's foundation.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert at least the 'downright bumpkin dandy—a fellow that, in the dog-days, will mow his two acres in buckskin gloves' phrase before the Hay-Seed exclamation to preserve the satirical voice.

findings.source_passage: Had it not been for us whalemen, that tract of land would this day perhaps have been in as howling condition as the coast of Labrador. As it is, parts of her back country are enough to frighten one, they look so bony.
findings.source_locator: Paragraph 5, after 'Not at all. Still New Bedford is a queer place.'
findings.why_it_matters: This is interpretively weighted: Ishmael's 'us whalemen' is an early moment of narrator self-identification with the whaling community, and the Labrador/bony back-country contrast anchors the chapter's ironic portrait of wealth-from-desolation. Its omission loses a key thematic note.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'us whalemen' clause and the Labrador/bony-back-country lines; they are short enough to include without exceeding compression budget.

findings.source_passage: And the women of New Bedford, they bloom like their own red roses. But roses only bloom in summer; whereas the fine carnation of their cheeks is perennial as sunlight in the seventh heavens. Elsewhere match that bloom of theirs, ye cannot, save in Salem, where they tell me the young girls breathe such musk, their sailor sweethearts smell them miles off shore, as though they were drawing nigh the odorous Moluccas instead of the Puritanic sands.
findings.source_locator: Final paragraph of the source segment
findings.why_it_matters: This closing paragraph is the chapter's most lyrically extravagant passage — the Salem musk/Moluccas conceit is a celebrated comic-erotic flourish and the segment's tonal capstone. Its complete omission leaves the draft ending on the horse-chestnuts, stripping the chapter of its memorable exit.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore at minimum 'the women of New Bedford, they bloom like their own red roses' and the Salem/Moluccas sentence as the chapter's closing lines; this is the segment's most quotable passage.

summary: Four medium-severity failures — the Broadway/Regent Street global-comic buildup, the bumpkin-dandy satirical setup, the 'us whalemen'/Labrador interpretive self-identification, and the entire Salem/Moluccas closing flourish — collectively erase the chapter's distinctive satirical voice and its memorable lyrical coda, triggering regeneration.
